text:
President Donald Trump said Sunday that the U.S. and Canada could settle their ongoing tariff dispute “pretty soon,” raising hopes of relief for businesses caught in the trade standoff. Speaking at a political rally in Port Huron, Michigan, Trump suggested Canada was ready to make major concessions, although he offered no details about a possible agreement.
“We’ll have that settled pretty soon. They’re willing to give us anything at this moment,” Trump told supporters.
The comments could be welcome news for U.S. automakers, particularly General Motors (GM) and Ford Motor Company (F), whose North American operations rely on cross-border supply chains. Tariffs on Canadian goods can raise production costs and put pressure on profit margins, especially when parts cross the border during vehicle manufacturing.
Michigan has been feeling the strain. The state is home to much of the U.S. auto industry, making trade tensions with Canada a particularly sensitive issue for local manufacturers and workers.
Trump’s Canada Tariffs Raise Concerns for U.S. Automakers
Trump defended his tariffs at the rally, arguing that Canada has taken advantage of the U.S. in trade. He also maintained that the measures are needed to protect American manufacturing. Yet even some Republicans have concerns about their impact on the auto sector.
Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers praised Trump’s tariffs for helping attract manufacturing investments from Chevrolet and Detroit Diesel. But he acknowledged that the auto-related measures remain a concern.
“The automobile portion of these Canadian tariffs worries me a little bit,” Rogers said during an appearance on NBC‘s Meet the Press.
For automakers, a deal that eases tariffs could help lower costs and improve the outlook for margins. The size of any benefit would depend on which duties are removed and when the changes take effect.
Trump’s comments didn’t offer a timeline beyond “pretty soon,” and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office had not immediately responded to Reuters’ request for comment. As of now, no specific concessions, tariff cuts, or agreement terms have been announced.
